text: Here is one small graph with seven nodes, drawn twice.
On the left runs breadth first search, on the right depth first.
Each keeps a frontier: a queue on the left, a stack on the right.
A queue hands back its oldest item, a stack its newest.
Both searches begin by putting node one into their frontier.
BFS takes node one from the queue, and adds two and three.
DFS takes node one from the stack, and pushes two and three.
BFS takes two from the front, adding new neighbors four and five.
DFS takes three off the top, since it went on last.
BFS takes three next, adding its new neighbors six and seven.
DFS pushed six and seven, so seven comes off the top.
BFS reaches four, a leaf, so nothing new joins the queue.
DFS takes six, also a leaf, leaving only two on the stack.
BFS takes five, another leaf, with six and seven still queued.
DFS finally backs up to two, and pushes four and five.
BFS takes six from the front, leaving only seven in the queue.
Five went on last, so DFS takes five before four.
BFS takes seven, and its queue is finally empty.
DFS takes four, and its stack is empty too.
The code was identical: only the queue and the stack differ.
BFS visited the nodes in the order one through seven.
DFS finished the whole right branch before it came back to two.
BFS sweeps level by level, in order of distance from the start.
DFS commits to one branch and follows it all the way down.
Both visit each node once, so the cost is nodes plus edges.
A queue spreads the search wide, while a stack sends it deep.
